s: I spy with my little eye; the phrase used in the guessing game “I spy” (in the German version, the hint is the colour of the object)

ich sehe was, was du nicht siehst.et: Literally, “I see something that you don't see”. Compare Dutch ik zie, ik zie wat jij niet ziet.

used to form adjectives, generally from nouns
-icht.et: From Middle High German -eht, from Old High German -ohti, -ahti. Cognate with Alemannic German -et, Bavarian -at, East Central German -it.

s: used to form collective nouns from adjectives, nouns and verbs
Rohr (“tube, reed”) + -icht → Röhricht n (“bush of reed”)
-icht.et: From Middle High German -ech, -ach, from Old High German -āhi. Paragogic -t after a final fricative is fairly common in Modern German (e.g. sonst, Saft); in this case likely reinforced by confusion with etymology 1 above.
